content: Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) is a surgical procedure that involves the complete removal of the penile foreskin. It has been shown to significantly reduce the risk of heterosexually acquired HIV infection in men. Evidence from three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) demonstrated a 60% reduction in HIV incidence among circumcised men, leading to the World Health Organization's (WHO) 2007 recommendation of VMMC as an additional HIV prevention strategy. Follow-up studies confirmed this protective effect, with a 66% reduction in HIV risk over six years. Observational studies conducted between 1986 and 2017 further supported these findings, showing a 50% lower risk of HIV infection in circumcised men. Among high-risk populations, such as men with HIV-positive partners or those in serodiscordant relationships, the risk reduction was even greater, at 71%. Community-based studies before and during the scale-up of VMMC programs also demonstrated significant reductions in HIV incidence, particularly in settings with high HIV prevalence. VMMC programs have been implemented alongside other HIV prevention strategies, such as antiretroviral therapy (ART). In communities where both VMMC and ART coverage increased, HIV prevalence was 44% lower in circumcised men compared to uncircumcised men. Modeling studies estimate that the nearly 23 million circumcisions performed by 2018 in 15 priority countries in East and Southern Africa averted approximately 250,000 new HIV infections. This number is expected to grow, with projections suggesting that VMMC could prevent up to 5 million infections by 2030. VMMC is a cost-effective intervention, particularly in regions with high HIV prevalence, as it reduces the lifetime costs associated with ART. It also provides lifelong partial protection against HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including human papillomavirus (HPV), herpes simplex virus-2, bacterial vaginosis, and Trichomonas vaginalis. Women benefit indirectly from VMMC programs due to the reduced risk of HIV transmission from circumcised male partners. Additionally, women may experience a lower risk of acquiring HIV from an HIV-positive circumcised partner, except during the initial healing period after circumcision. To maximize the benefits of VMMC, it is essential to integrate it into comprehensive HIV prevention programs. These programs should include education on safer sex practices, condom promotion, HIV testing services, and STI management. VMMC services also serve as an entry point for linking men to other health services, such as HIV care and treatment. For adolescent boys aged 15–19, consent procedures must align with the legal age for minor surgery in each country. Despite the significant impact of VMMC, challenges remain in achieving universal ART coverage and addressing gaps in HIV treatment services. Suboptimal adherence to ART, service delivery limitations, and drug resistance can reduce the effectiveness of HIV prevention efforts. Sustained attention to improving the quality of HIV treatment services is critical to achieving global targets. In addition to its role in HIV prevention, VMMC has broader health benefits. It reduces the risk of cervical cancer in women by lowering HPV transmission rates. Modeling studies suggest that scaling up VMMC could prevent approximately 20% of cervical cancer cases in scenarios with limited HPV vaccination and cervical cancer screening. Furthermore, VMMC programs provide opportunities to deliver other health services, such as cervical cancer screening and counseling for female partners, thereby addressing the health needs of both men and women. In summary, VMMC is a highly effective and cost-efficient intervention for reducing HIV incidence and improving public health outcomes. Its integration into combination prevention strategies, alongside ART and other measures, is essential for achieving global HIV prevention goals and controlling the epidemic.
